What exact structure is supposed to buy us

29 July 2026 · programme note

A research programme is not made coherent by repeating the same mathematical vocabulary. It becomes coherent when the same discipline of calculation survives across different physical problems.

The word exact is easily romanticised. It can suggest that a closed formula is valuable merely because it closes, or that an algebraic structure becomes physical merely because it is elegant. Neither is enough. For me, exactness is useful when it removes an ambiguity: when the geometry fixes a field, a source, a distance, a phase, a scalar sector, or an obstruction that can then be checked.

Structure is an input, not a conclusion

The inputs in my work vary. They include homogeneous spaces and conformal compactifications, spectral triples and finite calculi, quantum-Riemannian connections, matrix models, and Clifford or division-algebraic data. These structures do not all belong to one formalism, and forcing them into one would be artificial. What they share is rigidity. Once the input is chosen, there should be less freedom downstream, not more.

That is why the calculation in the middle matters. In field theory it may be a symmetry reduction followed by an exact stress tensor or source analysis. In spectral geometry it may be a variational computation of Connes distance. In finite geometry it may be the determination of one-forms, real structures, and inner fluctuations. In black-hole geometry it may be an amplitude flow and its accumulated phase. The calculation is where attractive language is forced to become a mathematical statement.

Several laboratories, one standard of evidence

This gives the programme several laboratories. Exact Yang–Mills and Maxwell fields test sources, charges, defects, trajectories, and transport. Quantum geometry tests horizon flow, geometric phase, and emergent gravitational equations. Spectral and information geometry tests whether an abstract metric agrees with operational distinguishability. Finite particle geometry asks which internal structures are required by the geometry and which have merely been inserted by hand.

The outputs are different, but the standard is the same. A phase must be computed. A charge must be conserved. A distance must be compared with an operational one. A finite geometry must disclose its allowed fields and its obstructions. If the result remains only suggestive, it belongs to the programme’s frontier, not to its list of established conclusions.

This is the sense in which I use the phrase “exact geometry as a generator of physics”: algebra and geometry supply constrained inputs, but physics is what remains after the calculation.
